content: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a severe and progressive condition that often results in right heart failure and premature death. Endothelin receptor antagonists (ERAs) have demonstrated efficacy in managing this condition. This review aimed to assess the effectiveness of ERAs in treating PAH. The study included randomized and quasi-randomized trials involving patients with PAH. A total of 17 randomized controlled trials with 3322 participants were analyzed. Most trials were short-term, lasting between 12 weeks and six months. Sixteen of these trials were placebo-controlled, with nine evaluating non-selective ERAs and seven assessing selective ERAs. The primary outcomes measured included exercise capacity (six-minute walk distance, 6MWD), functional class (based on WHO or NYHA criteria), Borg dyspnoea scores, dyspnoea-fatigue ratings, and mortality. Participants treated with ERAs were able to walk an average of 25.06 meters further in the six-minute walk test compared to those receiving placebo (95% confidence interval [CI] 17.13 to 32.99 meters; moderate-certainty evidence). ERAs also likely improved the functional class of more participants (odds ratio [OR] 1.41, 95% CI 1.16 to 1.70; moderate-certainty evidence) and reduced the likelihood of functional class deterioration (OR 0.43, 95% CI 0.26 to 0.72; moderate-certainty evidence) compared to placebo. There was a possible reduction in mortality with ERA treatment (OR 0.78, 95% CI 0.58 to 1.07; low-certainty evidence). Additionally, ERAs likely improved cardiopulmonary hemodynamics and may have reduced Borg dyspnoea scores in symptomatic patients. Hepatic toxicity was not common but may have been increased by ERA treatment, with an estimated rise from 37 to 67 cases per 1000 patients over 25 weeks (OR 1.88, 95% CI 0.91 to 3.90; moderate-certainty evidence). Although ERAs were generally well-tolerated, there were reports of irreversible liver failure associated with sitaxsentan, leading to its withdrawal from global markets. This underscores the importance of regular hepatic monitoring in patients receiving ERA therapy. Subgroup analyses comparing selective and non-selective ERAs did not reveal significant differences in most outcomes, except for mean pulmonary artery pressure. The data suggest that ERAs are particularly effective in patients with idiopathic pulmonary hypertension. However, their impact on reducing dyspnoea and mortality appears to be less pronounced. In conclusion, for patients with PAH classified as WHO functional class II or III, ERAs likely improve exercise capacity, functional class, and cardiopulmonary hemodynamics while preventing functional class deterioration. The combined use of ERAs and phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors may offer additional benefits, but further research is needed to confirm this. The risk of hepatic toxicity, particularly with sitaxsentan, highlights the necessity of careful liver function monitoring during ERA treatment.
